what_its_for: Paroxetine is used to treat depression, anxiety disorders (including panic attacks, social anxiety, and generalized anxiety), obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), and certain mood disorders. The brand Brisdelle is used specifically to treat hot flashes related to menopause. It works by increasing the amount of serotonin, a natural mood-balancing chemical, in your brain.
how_to_take: Take paroxetine by mouth, usually once a day, in the morning with or without food. If it upsets your stomach, try taking it with food or milk. Swallow the extended-release (CR) tablets whole — do not crush, chew, or break them. You may shake the liquid form gently before measuring your dose. Use a medicine measuring spoon or cup, not a regular kitchen spoon, to get the right amount.
dosing: Your doctor will start you on a low dose and slowly increase it to find what works best for you. Typical starting doses range from 10 mg to 20 mg once daily, and doses may be increased up to 60 mg per day depending on your condition. Always follow your doctor's specific instructions. Never change your dose on your own without talking to your doctor first.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember — but only if it is still the same day. If it is close to the time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and continue with your regular schedule. Never take two doses at once to make up for a missed one. If you are unsure what to do, call your pharmacist or doctor.
storage: Store paroxetine at room temperature, between 59°F and 86°F (15°C to 30°C). Keep it away from heat, moisture, and direct light. Do not store it in the bathroom. Keep the liquid form tightly closed and do not freeze it. Keep all medications out of reach of children and pets. Do not flush unused medication down the toilet — ask your pharmacist about a safe medicine take-back program.
what_to_avoid: Avoid drinking alcohol while taking paroxetine, as it can increase drowsiness and make side effects worse. Do not take paroxetine if you are also taking MAO inhibitors (such as phenelzine, tranylcypromine, or linezolid) — this combination can cause a dangerous and potentially life-threatening reaction. Do not stop taking paroxetine suddenly without your doctor's guidance, as this can cause withdrawal symptoms like dizziness, nausea, tingling, anxiety, and irritability. Avoid driving or operating heavy machinery until you know how this medication affects you, as it may cause drowsiness or dizziness. Tell your doctor about all other medications, vitamins, and supplements you take, as paroxetine can interact with many drugs including blood thinners, other antidepressants, and certain pain relievers like ibuprofen or aspirin.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you experience: thoughts of suicide or self-harm (especially in the first few weeks of treatment or after a dose change), unusual changes in mood or behavior, agitation, restlessness, feeling unusually excited or aggressive, severe dizziness or fainting, irregular or fast heartbeat, severe nausea or vomiting, seizures, signs of low sodium levels (headache, confusion, weakness, trouble concentrating), or signs of serotonin syndrome (rapid heart rate, high fever, muscle stiffness or twitching, loss of coordination, or severe agitation). Also contact your doctor if you develop skin rash, unusual bruising or bleeding, or if your symptoms do not improve after several weeks.
when_it_works: Paroxetine does not work right away. Most people start to notice some improvement in sleep, appetite, and energy within 1 to 2 weeks. However, it usually takes 4 to 6 weeks of regular use to feel the full benefit for mood, anxiety, or other symptoms. Be patient and keep taking it as directed, even if you do not feel better right away. Do not stop taking it without talking to your doctor first.
special_populations: Older adults (65 and over): Paroxetine may cause more dizziness or drowsiness in older people, increasing the risk of falls. Lower starting doses are often recommended. Pregnant women: Paroxetine may cause harm to an unborn baby, especially if taken in the first trimester. It has also been linked to rare heart defects in newborns. Talk to your doctor about the risks and benefits if you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant. Breastfeeding: Small amounts of paroxetine pass into breast milk. Discuss this with your doctor before breastfeeding. Children and teenagers: Paroxetine is not approved for use in children under 18 years old for most conditions. Young people may have an increased risk of suicidal thoughts when starting antidepressants. Close monitoring is very important. Kidney or liver problems: Your doctor may need to start you on a lower dose if you have kidney or liver disease.
